module.title: Modals of Probability & Deduction: Must, Might, Can't in Everyday Reasoning
module.objective: Menggunakan kata kerja bantu modal untuk menyimpulkan kepastian (must), kemungkinan (might/could), dan kemustahilan (can't).

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Mysteries in Everyday Life
subModules.grammarFocus: Modals of Probability and Deduction (Must, Might, Can't)

content.summary: Welcome to your reading mission on modal verbs of deduction. In this module, you will learn how to read short investigative stories and everyday mysteries while figuring out how people use clues to make logical guesses about situations around them.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Modal verbs of deduction and probability (must, might, could, can't) followed by base verbs.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Terms related to logical reasoning, clues, and solving everyday situations.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for logical connectors and specific evidence within narrative paragraphs to confirm deductions.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short B1 stories involving everyday detective work and mysteries.
Locate specific clues and details that explain character behavior.
Recognize and apply grammar patterns with must, might, and can't to show levels of certainty.

contextWarmup.prompt: You see your neighbor walking his dog at 6:00 AM on a Sunday. What is the most logical deduction?
options: He must really love early morning walks because his dog needs exercise.
He can't like animals at all.
He might be sleeping right now.
contextWarmup.explanation: If you see him walking the dog in person, it is a logical deduction with high certainty that he is up early for his dog's routine.

rules: MUST + bare infinitive = positive deduction with high certainty (99% sure). Formula: Subject + must + verb. Example: 'The lights are on. He must be home.'
MIGHT/COULD + bare infinitive = deduction with medium probability (50% sure). Formula: Subject + might/could + verb. Example: 'She is not answering her phone. She might be in a meeting.'
CAN'T + bare infinitive = negative deduction with high certainty (almost impossible). Formula: Subject + can't + verb. Example: 'That can't be John. He is in London today.'

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mix up 'must' for deduction with 'must' or 'have to' for obligation. In deduction, 'must' means 'I am sure this is true based on evidence', whereas 'have to' is a rule.
commonTrap.wrong: He must to be at work because his car is gone.
commonTrap.correct: He must be at work because his car is gone. (No 'to' after modal verbs)

content.passageTitle: The Mystery of the Empty Office
paragraphs: It was Monday morning at the marketing agency, and Sarah walked into the office expecting a busy room. Instead, all the lights were turned off, and the desks were completely quiet. She looked around for any sign of her colleagues, but nobody was at their computers. She noticed a cup of hot coffee steaming on Mark desk. Because the coffee was still warm, she knew that Mark must have been there only a few minutes before.

Sarah checked her phone for any messages about a sudden meeting, but her inbox was empty. She wondered where everyone could be. They might have gone to the emergency meeting room downstairs, or they could be testing the new projector in the auditorium. However, she remembered that the auditorium was closed for repairs today. That meant they can't be in the auditorium. Suddenly, she heard laughter coming from the kitchen and smiled.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Solving the Mystery of the Missing Colleague

content.summary: Focus on listening for clues and modal verbs of deduction like must, might, and can't. When speakers are sure about something, they use must. When they are certain something is impossible, they use can't. When they are unsure, they use might or could.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about deducing situations.
Identify details such as reasons, evidence, and logical conclusions.
Notice how words link together in connected speech during rapid dialogue.

keyPhrases.note: Used when you are almost 90 percent sure based on strong evidence.
Used when you are sure something is impossible.
Used to express a possibility that is around 50 percent likely.
Synonymous with might, used for alternative possibilities.

connectedSpeech.note: The /t/ in must drops out before the consonant /b/.
Native speakers emphasize the strong /t/ in can't to show disbelief.
Do you reduces to dya in casual spoken English.
The preposition at becomes a weak schwa sound.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Modals of Probability and Deduction

content.summary: Master writing sentences that express logical deductions and probability using must, might, and can't based on clues in your environment.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: High Certainty Deduction
blueprintItems.example: The windows are frosted. It must be very cold outside.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Moderate Possibility Deduction
blueprintItems.example: Sarah is not at her desk. She might be in the meeting room.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Impossible Deduction
blueprintItems.example: Mark is in New York. That can't be him walking across the street here.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use the bare infinitive without 'to' after modal verbs like must, might, and can't.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He must to be tired after the long journey.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He must be tired after the long journey.
mechanicsRules.why: Modal verbs must be followed directly by the base form of the verb without the particle 'to'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'can't' for negative deductions of certainty, not 'mustn't'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She left five minutes ago. She mustn't be far away.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She left five minutes ago. She can't be far away.
mechanicsRules.why: In English, 'mustn't' expresses prohibition, while 'can't' expresses logical impossibility.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always place modal verbs of deduction directly after the subject of the sentence.
mechanicsRules.badExample: In the office must be someone because the lights are on.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Someone must be in the office because the lights are on.
mechanicsRules.why: English sentences require the subject to come before the modal verb in standard deduction statements.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'must' to show high certainty:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I am certain that pizza is delicious because it smells amazing.
targetAnswers: That pizza must be delicious because it smells amazing.
The pizza must be delicious because it smells amazing.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Replace 'I am certain that' with the subject followed by 'must be'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'can't' to show impossibility:
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is impossible that John is sleeping because I hear him playing the guitar.
targetAnswers: John can't be sleeping because I hear him playing the guitar.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Replace 'It is impossible that [Subject] is' with '[Subject] can't be'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'might' to show possibility:
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is possible that Lisa will join us for dinner later.
targetAnswers: Lisa might join us for dinner later.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Replace 'It is possible that [Subject] will' with '[Subject] might'.

practicumQuestions.promptText: The lights are all turned off, so they ___ be home.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the modal for negative certainty.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When lights are off, it is almost certain they are not home, so 'can't' is required.

practicumQuestions.promptText: I am not sure where my keys are. They ___ be in the kitchen drawer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When uncertain, 'might' or 'could' expresses a moderate possibility.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a deduction sentence using 'must' based on this clue: 'The street is completely flooded.'

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a deduction sentence using 'might' based on this clue: 'Anna is not answering her phone.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: Anna is not answering her phone.
practicumQuestions.hint: Example: She might be busy driving.
targetAnswers: She might be in a meeting.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'might be' to offer a reasonable explanation for an unanswered phone.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Transform the statement into a negative deduction using 'can't': 'I am sure Mark is not the thief.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: I am sure Mark is not the thief.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Replace 'I am sure [Subject] is not' with '[Subject] can't be'.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Modals of Probability and Deduction

content.summary: This module focuses on speaking clearly when expressing deduction and probability in everyday conversations. You will learn how to use modal verbs like must, might, and can't with appropriate sentence stress and intonation to convey different levels of certainty.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to weak forms and contractions. In rapid spoken English, modal verbs are often unstressed unless you want to emphasize contrast or certainty. Focus on clear consonant endings for words like must and can't.

pillars.name: Modal Reduction
pillars.explanation: When speaking at a normal pace, auxiliary verbs such as might are pronounced with a schwa sound, while can't requires a sharp t stop.

pillars.name: Intonation in Deduction
pillars.target: Use rising and falling tones for logic
pillars.explanation: Use a falling tone when you are certain of your conclusion, and a rising tone when you are speculating or unsure.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how the primary stress remains on the second syllable across both word forms.
The stress shifts from the first syllable in probable to the third syllable in probability.
Both words maintain stress on the second syllable.
Stress remains firmly on the first syllable in both the adjective and noun forms.

drills.targetText: She left her jacket here, so she must be nearby.
drills.phonetic: /ʃiː lɛft hɜː ˈdʒækɪt hɪə, səʊ ʃiː mʌst biː ˈnɪəbaɪ/
drills.hint: Keep your voice firm on must to show certainty.

drills.targetText: He might join us later if he finishes his work.
drills.phonetic: /hiː maɪt dʒɔɪn ʌs ˈleɪtə ɪf hiː ˈfɪnɪʃɪz hɪz wɜːk/
drills.hint: Soften your tone on might to indicate uncertainty.

drills.targetText: That can't be true because I saw him at home.
drills.phonetic: /ðæt kɑːnt biː truː bɪˈkɒz aɪ sɔː hɪm æt həʊm/
drills.hint: Pronounce the final t in can't clearly.

drills.targetText: Based on the evidence, this conclusion makes sense.
drills.phonetic: /beɪst ɒn ði ˈɛvɪdəns, ðɪs kənˈkluːʒən meɪks sɛns/
drills.hint: Pause slightly after evidence to structure your thought.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about a time you had to make a deduction based on clues.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell me about a situation when you found a clue and had to guess what happened.
storyPoints: What object or clue you discovered
What deduction you made using must or might
What the actual truth turned out to be
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I found muddy shoes by the door, so I deduced that my brother must have gone hiking.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ faʊnd ˈmʌdi ʃuːz baɪ ðə dɔː/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Speak fluently in full sentences while describing past deductions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about a mysterious noise you heard at night.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Describe a time you heard a strange sound and what you thought it was.
storyPoints: When and where you heard the unusual sound
What modal of probability you used to explain it
How you felt after finding out the source
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I heard a scratch on the window, and I thought it might be a stray cat.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Maintain a steady pace and use descriptive language.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Discuss an unexpected package delivery with a neighbor.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Plan an outdoor picnic with your classmate.

practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Suggest that it might rain later in the afternoon.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It might rain later, so we could postpone our picnic until tomorrow.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a moderate tone to express conditional probability.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use the target vocabulary word 'deduction' in a complete spoken sentence.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say a sentence explaining your logical deduction about a puzzle.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My deduction is based on the footprints we found near the garden gate.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Pronounce deduction with correct syllable stress on the second syllable.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Form a sentence using the modal structure 'must have' plus past participle.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Make a sentence about something someone finished in the past with certainty.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: She must have finished the report because her computer is turned off.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure you blend 'must have' naturally in speech without overemphasizing 'have'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read aloud the sentence focusing on correct syllable stress for 'probability'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Pronounce the word probability clearly within this sentence.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: There is a high probability that the train will arrive on time.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɛr ɪz ə haɪ ˌprɒb.əˈbɪl.ə.ti ðæt ðə treɪn wɪl əˈraɪv/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Place primary stress on the third syllable of probability.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read the sentence with a falling intonation to express absolute certainty.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say this sentence with a definite falling tone at the end.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: It is impossible for him to have solved the riddle so quickly.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪt ɪz ɪmˈpɒs.ə.bəl fɔːhɪm tuː hæv sɒlvd ðə ˈrɪd.əl/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Lower your pitch at the end of the sentence to show strong conviction.
